Title: SymphonyGen: 3D Hierarchical Orchestral Generation with Controllable Harmony Skeleton

ABSTRACT
Generating symphonic music requires simultaneously man-
aging high-level structural form and dense, multi-track
orchestration. Existing symbolic models often struggle
with a “complexity-control imbalance”, in which scal-
ing bottlenecks limit long-term granular steerability. We
present SymphonyGen, a 3D hierarchical framework for
contemporary cinematic orchestration. SymphonyGen em-
ploys a cascading decoder architecture that decomposes
the Bar, Track, and Event axes, improving computational
efficiency and scalability over conventional 1D or 2D mod-
els. We introduce “short-score” conditioning via a beat-
quantized multi-voice harmony skeleton, enabling outline
control while preserving textural diversity.
The model
is further refined using Group Relative Policy Optimiza-
tion (GRPO) with a cross-modal audio-perceptual reward,
aligning symbolic output with modern acoustic expecta-
tions. Additionally, we implement a dissonance-averse
sampling algorithm to suppress unintended tonal clashes
during inference. Objective evaluations show that both
reinforcement learning and dissonance-averse sampling ef-
fectively enhance harmonic cleanliness while maintaining
melodic expression. Subjective evaluations demonstrate
that SymphonyGen outperforms baselines in musicality and
preference for orchestral music generation. Demo page:
https://symphonygen.github.io/
1. INTRODUCTION
For centuries, symphonic composition has served as the pri-
mary vehicle for expansive musical storytelling through the
collective power of the orchestra. Replicating this complex-
ity, however, remains a formidable challenge for symbolic
AI, as it demands the simultaneous management of high-
level form and multi-track textures. Specifically, models are
required to capture dependencies across dozens of voices
while maintaining a sophisticated, evolving harmonic land-
scape over long temporal horizons. Toward this goal, con-
siderable progress has been achieved through the adoption

of Transformer architectures [1,2] and the development of
symbolic musical representations [3,4]. Frameworks such
as SymphonyNet [5] have employed permutation-invariant
modeling for symphonic scores, while more recent models
like NotaGen [6] leverage large language model (LLM)
training paradigms to generate classical scores with impres-
sive fidelity.
However, while these models effectively capture charac-
teristic patterns of target styles, they often treat generation
as a monolithic sequence modeling problem that overlooks
intermediate structural decisions, such as the use of a piano-
reduction sketch. This neglect of the multi-stage workflows
inherent to professional production leaves a critical gap in
controllable symphonic creation, which we characterize as
a “complexity-control imbalance”. On one hand, many ap-
proaches for orchestral composition or arrangement [7–12]
flatten multi-track scores into unidimensional token streams,
leading to scaling bottlenecks that hinder progress in large-
scale orchestral generation. On the other, prevailing control
mechanisms [13–17] remain insufficient for decomposing
the task into workflows that support deep human-AI col-
laboration. Furthermore, models trained on broad MIDI
datasets frequently produce spurious dissonance, failing to

achieve the acoustic clarity and aesthetic value required for
cinematic-grade orchestral composition.
To bridge these gaps, we present SymphonyGen, a hier-
archical framework controlled by a multi-voice harmony
skeleton for contemporary cinematic orchestration. To the
best of our knowledge, this is the first work that specifically
targets symbolic cinematic orchestration rather than general
orchestration. Our central contributions are:
• 3D Hierarchical Architecture: A cascading encoder-
decoder system that processes the Bar, Track, and
Event axes separately, reducing computational over-
head while improving multi-track scalability.
• Multi-Voice Harmony Skeleton: A novel “short-
score” condition that provides a granular music outline,
steering the composition through beat-quantized har-
monic and melodic contours.
• Audio-Perceptual RL: A reinforcement pipeline uti-
lizing a cross-modal reward. By aligning symbolic
output with acoustic perception, this approach miti-
gates the qualitative limitations of MIDI datasets.
• Dissonance-Averse Sampling: A logit-adjustment
algorithm that references the harmony skeleton to sup-
press unintended clashes during inference, especially
those between the non-harmonic tones.
2. RELATED WORK
2.1 Symbolic Orchestral Generation
Generative models specifically targeting orchestral music
are less common than those for general multi-track tasks.
Early efforts like MuseGAN [18] utilized GANs, but the
field has largely shifted toward Transformers to capture
long-range dependencies. Pop Music Transformer [3] and
Compound Word Transformer [4] introduced fundamental
tokenization schemes that remain influential.
SymphonyNet [5] pioneered the task of symphonic gen-
eration and introduced a large-scale symphony dataset.
More recently, NotaGen [6] leveraged CLaMP-DPO to gen-
erate high-fidelity classical scores. While successful, these
models operate as single-stage generators that limit human
collaboration.
2.2 Music Arrangement and Orchestration
Automatic orchestration is the process of expanding or
transforming musical material into an ensemble version.
Early data-driven approaches like AccoMontage [7,19] and
MuseMorphose [8] focused on accompaniment and style
transfer, with the latter introducing bar-level control over
polyphonic density. METEOR [9] extended these concepts
to the orchestral domain while utilizing a melody-aware
Transformer-VAE. Subsequent advancements include style
prior modeling [10] and sequence-to-sequence frameworks
that utilize multiple conditional streams [11].
Despite these developments, arrangement models are
often built on VAE latent spaces to mitigate the scarcity

conditions are mainly analyzed from the input music, while
our condition comes from diverse sources (Figure 1).
2.3 Controllable and Structured Music Generation
Fine-grained control is essential for professional AI mu-
sic. FIGARO [13] utilized bar-level interpretable features
for controllable generation, while Theme Transformer [14]
focused on thematic conditioning. To address phrase struc-
ture, researchers have proposed structure-related attention
mechanisms [15] and cascaded diffusion models for whole-
song generation [16]. Additionally, Text2midi [17] explored
generating symbolic music from text captions.
While previous methods offer diverse conditions for
steering music generation, they still lack the detailed multi-
voice grounding that could greatly enhance control for com-
plex symphonic orchestration. In contrast, our approach
more effectively bridges compositional intent with orches-
tral realization by outlining the harmony skeleton.
3. METHODOLOGY
3.1 3D Hierarchical Architecture
The backbone of our model is a series of cascading Trans-
former encoders and decoders to process one structural level
at a time. This hierarchical approach of decomposing the
sequence into Bar, Track, and Event levels is designed to
manage the high density of symphonic scores. (We define
events as the sequence of tokenized musical notes or note
attributes within a specific bar-track intersection.)
While 2D models (e.g., NotaGen) divide tokens into
patches, our 3D architecture groups notes by bars and
tracks. As shown in Table 1, the 3D architecture scales
quadratically with respect to each axis independently, and
substantially reduces inference VRAM peak usage. This
decomposition is particularly effective when coupled with
a music outline provider such as our harmony skeleton; by
delegating global planning to the skeleton, the model cir-
cumvents the exhaustive computation typically required to
maintain coherence across a flattened representation.
3.2 Harmony Skeleton Analysis
We employ a rule-based analysis of beat-wise harmony
skeleton that consists of two steps:


Figure 2. Model architecture. The pretrained model is supervised by a total loss L = 0.05Lmeta + 0.5Lharm + Lmusic.
Chord Template Matching. We select a template chord
(any triads or seventh chords) based on the highest cosine
similarity of the pitch-class distribution for each beat.
Extension Identification. We employ dynamic program-
ming to include a maximal set of additional notes as chord
extensions, under the constraint of no new minor or major
second intervals being introduced.
The chordal notes and the extensions are stretched to
beat boundaries to form the harmony skeleton. Roughly
speaking, the harmony skeleton specifies what pitches are
allowed to be used in the music as harmonic tones.
We tested the harmony skeleton analysis method on the
DCML harmony annotation corpus [20], achieving about
85% pitch-class precision and 89% pitch-class recall.
3.3 Encoding and Decoding
The model operates via a consistent process of transforma-
tion, where higher-level encoded features are decoded into
contexts to guide lower-level decoders (Figure 2).
We first process harmony events (grouped by bars)
through an event encoder with pooling to produce harmony
bar features. Simultaneously, music events are processed by
a shared event encoder to produce track features, while fus-
ing metadata embeddings (bar length, track ID, instrument
ID). The track features are processed by a track encoder to
produce music bar features.

3.4 Two-Stream Cross-Attention
A flexible cross-attention mechanism for the music event
decoder is important for our architecture to maintain struc-
tural coherence. Odd layers cross-attend to the harmony
event context of the current bar, while even layers cross-
attend to the output hidden states of the preceding layer,
retrieved from the previous bar in a track-aligned manner
(Figure 3). As the set of active tracks may vary across bars,
we utilize an auxiliary Track-Previous Index Map to help a
track “find itself” in the previous bar even if its index has
shifted. During inference, the track-previous index map is
updated as track IDs are predicted.
In an ablation study, the two-stream cross-attention
mechanism reduced about 30% of validation loss compared
to using either one stream in isolation.
3.5 Tokenization and Metadata Handling
To balance the ratios of padding and truncation of the 3D
music representation, we propose a compressed REMI [3]
tokenization scheme. It utilizes five types of tokens: Pitch,


Figure 3. Hidden state retrieval from the previous bar.
Figure 4. Tokenization Compression Scheme.
Position, Duration, End-of-Track, and a novel Legato. The
compression follows three steps (Figure 4):
Note Grouping. Notes at the same position share the
same position token. Notes with the same duration at the
same position share the same duration token.
Downbeat Pruning. We treat [Pos: 0] as the implicit
default position for each bar, omitting the downbeat tokens.
Legato Fusion. We compress tokens where a note starts
immediately after the previous one ends. A [Legato: d]
token at position p serves as a “mini-BPE” that replaces the
original [Dur: d] and [Pos: p+d] tokens.
Currently, our model processes 32 bars of music at a
time, where each bar contains up to 32 tracks and each track
up to 32 events. For the harmony skeleton, each bar contains
up to 64 events. Using the compressed tokenization, most
event sequences in the dataset fit in the respective limit (97%
for music, 98% for harmony). All positions and durations
are quantized to a 32nd-note grid.
Unlike standard models that tokenize metadata within
the main sequence, SymphonyGen employs separate heads
for predicting bar lengths, track IDs, instrument IDs, as
well as future extensions of metadata. The track ID head is
also responsible for predicting the End-of-Bar special track.
3.6 Reinforcement Learning via GRPO
After pretraining, the model is refined using Group Relative
Policy Optimization (GRPO) [21]. In each GRPO epoch,
we sample K harmony skeletons. For each skeleton, we
generate a group of G musical pieces. GRPO estimates
the advantage function by normalizing rewards within each
group, allowing the model to efficiently explore diverse
orchestration strategies by the same harmony condition.
The reward function is given by CLaMP 3 [22], a three-
way alignment model for text, audio, and music score. We
utilize its audio encoder to embed the audio converted from
MIDI outputs by MuseScore 3.6.2. After pooling, the co-
sine similarity against the centroid embedding of a reference
audio set serves as the reward.
This cross-modal reward has three primary advantages:
(1) it captures high-dimensional orchestral features that are
difficult to specify via rule-based rewards; (2) it bypasses
the “symbolic data bottleneck” by utilizing high-quality
audio recordings as the training signal; and (3) it uses a
reference set of different modality from the pretraining
dataset, thereby reducing plagiarism risks.
3.7 Dissonance-Averse Sampling
To combat the issue of spurious dissonance often found in
symbolic models, we implement inference-time dissonance-
averse sampling relative to a reference harmony. Since our
architecture maintains explicit knowledge of the harmony
skeleton that discerns harmonic (H) and non-harmonic (N)
tones at any time step t in the entire music, we can distin-
guish between different types of dissonances.
First, we define a symmetric dissonance matrix W,
where Wij ∈[0, 1] represents the degree of clash between
pitch i and pitch j. Then, we compute the following score:

where Ht and Nt are the normalized occupancy vectors of

The values in W are guided by interval sensory distance
as described in the Plomp-Levelt curve [23]; we set these
weights manually, where (for example) minor seconds and
tritones receive weights of 1.0 and 0.95, while perfect fifths
receive 0.1. To ensure acoustic clarity, W can be further
modulated by a register-dependent decay function to respect
the Low Interval Limit—a principle in orchestration that
necessitates wider intervals in lower registers.
During music event decoding, we subtract the logits
of pitch tokens by the amount of dissonance each pitch
would introduce at that time. The pitch logits are then
re-normalized, preserving the total probability mass.
4. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
4.1 Dataset
We utilize the SymphonyNet Dataset [5], comprising 728
classical and 45,632 contemporary MIDI files. The MIDI
files are partitioned into a 90/10 train/val split.
4.2 Training and Inference Details
SymphonyGen is implemented with 33 layers (512 hidden
size, 124M parameters), consisting of 8 harmony event
decoder layers, 9 music event decoder layers, and 4 layers
each for the rest of encoders and decoders. Pre-training
was conducted on four NVIDIA H800 GPUs for one day

In GRPO rollout and final inference, harmony skeletons

employ filters rejecting skeletons with low density (< 3

We set sampling parameters (λhn, λnn) to (1, 10), top-p
to 0.99 and temperature to 1.0. Pitch logits out of the instru-

music event decoding. The BPM is set to a constant 120.

4.4 Subjective Test Design
We conduct two rounds of subjective listening tests. The
first round focuses on composition against other orches-
tral generation models, and the second round against an
arrangement model. These baselines are:
• SymphonyNet (42M) [5]: A pioneer model in sym-
phony generation employing linear attention. We in-
clude representative official demo samples in the or-
chestral style, which are either conditioned on chord
labels or generated from scratch.
1 Detailed implementations will be available in our codebase.
• NotaGen (516M) [6]: A state-of-the-art symbolic
generation model reinforced with CLaMP2-DPO. We
compare against its latest version, NotaGen-X. We set
the style labels to (Romantic, Brahms/Dvoˇrák, Orches-
tral) and filter for high-density 32-bar windows (> 6
tracks) to ensure stylistic comparability.
• METEOR (67M) [9]: A melody-aware controllable
re-orchestration model. We include representative of-
ficial demo samples in the orchestral style, which are
conditioned on 8 bars of existing music.
We also compare against orchestral music excerpts selected
from the SymphonyNet Dataset. All participants rate sam-
ples on a 5-point Likert scale across four dimensions: Over-
all Quality, Musical Coherence, Orchestration Richness,
and Preference. We collect comments from the participants
to understand the prevailing styles of each model.
For the first round, we use harmony skeletons generated
from our model. For the second round, we use harmony
skeletons analyzed from the validation set. For both rounds,
we generate one sample per skeleton. We apply additional
skeleton filters requiring at least four V/V (7) →I/i ca-
dences in 32 bars and starting with major or minor chords.
We also prune the skeletons into pure template chords. We
consider the ability to easily apply diverse skeleton filters
to be an inherent advantage of our controllable framework.
5. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
5.1 Objective Evaluation
As shown in Table 2, the reinforcement learning stage sig-
nificantly enhances the average CLaMP score and lowers
dissonance scores, while preserving melodic movement and
ornament. This suggests that the model is more aligned with
modern acoustic expectations. Dissonance-averse sampling
further suppresses the non-harmonic artifacts.
As λhn and λnn increase, the melodic movement and
ornament reach their peak around (λhn, λnn) = (1, 10).
Beyond this “sweet spot” (e.g., at (5, 20)), the model be-
comes overly mechanical and stagnant, losing the legitimate
passing notes where musicality resides. This suggests that
mild H −N penalties combined with aggressive N −N
suppression yield the best balance between harmonic clean-
liness and melodic expression.

5.2 Subjective Evaluation
5.2.1 Round 1: Orchestral Composition Task
We collected 235 evaluations from 32 participants (10 ed-
ucated, 22 general). As shown in Table 3, SymphonyGen
captures most of the highest ratings across both groups.
General Listeners: Our model achieves a significant
lead in Quality, Coherence and Preference within this group.
This suggests that general listeners find SymphonyGen’s
contemporary cinematic style more accessible. Notably,
our model surpasses the average ratings of selected excerpts
from the dataset, which indicates that general listeners may
find the average MIDI data less “polished” than our RL-
aligned dissonance-reduced output.
Educated Listeners: While SymphonyGen remains
the preferred model, the performance gap narrows among
educated listeners. This convergence suggests that educated
listeners possess a higher cognitive tolerance for complex
harmonic tension or dissonance; they are more likely to
appreciate the structural intent of a piece even when certain
segments are harmonically compromised.
5.2.2 Round 2: Orchestral Arrangement Task
In light of our marginal lead in Orchestral Richness in
Round 1, we introduced a composite reward (CLaMP 3 +
0.2 × tanh(Track Density/4)) in the Round 2 test. We
also found it necessary to activate the register-dependent
decay in W to maintain clarity in the bass as track density
increased. We collected 96 evaluations from 16 participants
(all educated). The results are shown in Table 4.
SymphonyGen outperforms the baseline in all dimen-
sions, with a significant lead in Overall Quality and notice-
able lead in Orchestral Richness. This suggests that when
augmented with a track density reward, our model is able
to achieve richer orchestration while preserving musicality.
5.2.3 Qualitative Feedback
We have gathered comments from our participants to better
understand our model’s performance and limitations.
Strength: Participants more frequently described the
style of our model using expressions like “a strong sense
of fate”, “storytelling”, or as having evocative imagery.
This suggests that our model is more adept at cinematic
orchestration and conveying narrative emotions compared
to the baselines.
Weakness: Listeners still occasionally found that the
“harmony was strange” or contained “many mistakes”, with
others describing specific segments as “noisy” or “messy”.
This is likely due to errors in harmony skeleton generation.
In the Round 2 test, some participants noted the orches-
tration could feel “too full”. This indicates a limitation of
manual reward shaping.
6. CONCLUSION
This paper introduces SymphonyGen, a 3D hierarchical
framework designed to master the dual complexities of or-
chestral composition and arrangement. By decomposing the
Bar, Track, and Event axes, we achieve improved computa-
tional efficiency and scalability while maintaining structural
coherence. Our multi-voice harmony skeleton provides a
music outline to steer orchestration with granular precision.
By integrating audio-perceptual reinforcement learning and
dissonance-averse sampling, SymphonyGen successfully
produces cinematic scores that resonate more effectively
with general listeners.
This framework represents a substantial step toward pro-
fessional AI collaborators capable of handling the struc-
tural and textural demands of contemporary orchestral mu-
sic. Future work could improve by adding voice-leading
constraints to the harmony skeleton generation to reduce
uncanny horizontal transitions, as well as using diverse ref-
erence audio sets to learn structural layering and orchestral
breathing more dynamically.
7. ETHICS STATEMENT
Our training data consists of publicly available symbolic
music datasets and audio references. While SymphonyGen
automates aspects of orchestral composition, it is designed
as a collaborative tool to assist composers rather than com-
pete with them. We anticipate that human composers will
benefit more from our controllable framework than general
users or AI agents. Users should remain cognizant of po-
tential plagiarism risks inherent in generative models rather
than assuming all outputs are entirely novel. Finally, we
acknowledge that our “dissonance-averse” mechanism is
tuned to specific harmonic traditions and may not reflect
the aesthetic values of all musical cultures.

Abstract: Generating symphonic music requires simultaneously man- aging high-level structural form and dense, multi-track orchestration. Existing symbolic models often struggle with a “complexity-control imbalance”, in which scal- ing bottlenecks limit long-term granular steerability. We present SymphonyGen, a 3D hierarchical framework for contemporary cinematic orchestration. SymphonyGen em- ploys a cascading decoder architecture that decomposes the Bar, Track, and Event axes, improving computational efficiency and scalability over conventional 1D or 2D mod- els. We introduce “short-score” conditioning via a beat- quantized multi-voice harmony skeleton, enabling outline control while preserving textural diversity. The model is further refined using Group Relative Policy Optimiza- tion (GRPO) with a cross-modal audio-perceptual reward, aligning symbolic output with modern acoustic expecta- tions. Additionally, we implement a dissonance-averse sampling algorithm to suppress unintended tonal clashes during inference. Objective evaluations show that both reinforcement learning and dissonance-averse sampling ef- fectively enhance harmonic cleanliness while maintaining melodic expression. Subjective evaluations demonstrate that SymphonyGen outperforms baselines in musicality and preference for orchestral music generation. Demo page: https://symphonygen.github.io/
